transcription.tex: \textbf{Pure Mathematics Year 2}\par Chapter 10: Numerical Methods\par 1. Locating roots\par 2. Using iteration to approximate roots of \(f(x)=0\)\par 3. Introduction to the Newton–Raphson method

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: At GCSE you used iteration to obtain successively better approximations to solutions. We revisit this and introduce a more powerful method.
\textbf{1. Locating roots}\par Understand what a root is and when a root must lie in an interval.\par Show that \(f(x)=x^3-4x^2+3x+1\) has a root between \(x=1.4\) and \(x=1.5\).
\textbf{2. Iteration}\par Rearrange \(f(x)=0\) as \(x=g(x)\), then use \(x_{n+1}=g(x_n)\).
\textbf{3. Newton–Raphson}\par Follow tangents to approach a root, often faster:\[x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f^{\prime}(x_n)}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

slides.title: Why Do We Need Numerical Methods?

transcription.tex: Finding a root of \(f(x)\) means finding an input whose output is zero.
Solve \(f(x)=0\).
Some exact roots are complicated and difficult to calculate. For example, \(x^3+2x^2-3x+4=0\):
Other equations, such as \(x-\cos x=0\), have no standard exact algebraic formula for their root.
Use a numerical approximation: the root is approximately \(0.739085\).
Numerical methods give progressively better approximations to solutions of \(f(x)=0\).

slides.title: Proving a Solution Lies in an Interval

transcription.tex: Show that \(f(x)=e^x+2x-3\) has a root between \(x=0.5\) and \(x=0.6\).
If a continuous graph changes from negative to positive, its \(y\)-values must pass through zero.
\[f(0.5)=e^{0.5}+1-3=-0.351278\ldots<0,\]\[f(0.6)=e^{0.6}+1.2-3=0.022118\ldots>0.\]There is a change of sign, and \(f\) is continuous on \([0.5,0.6]\). Hence a root lies between 0.5 and 0.6.
\textbf{Exam tip}\par Calculate both endpoint values and explicitly state that there is a change of sign. Include continuity in the argument.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: A student claims: “For \(f(x)=1/x\), \(f(-1)=-1\) and \(f(1)=1\). There is a change of sign, so a root lies in \([-1,1]\).”
Why is the Genius wrong (again)?

The function is not continuous across this interval: it is undefined at \(x=0\), where there is a vertical asymptote. It never equals zero.\par A sign change guarantees a root only when the function is continuous throughout the interval. Otherwise the graph can pass from negative to positive without crossing the axis.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

slides.title: No Sign Change Does Not Mean No Root

transcription.tex: No sign change does \textbf{not} prove that an interval contains no roots.

The graph can cross the axis twice and return to the original sign. A graph can also touch the axis at a root without changing sign.\par The sign-change test can therefore miss roots: it gives a sufficient condition when continuity holds, not a necessary condition.

slides.title: Proving a Solution to a Given Accuracy

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C3 January 2013}\par \(g(x)=e^{x-1}+x-6\). The root of \(g(x)=0\) is \(\alpha\).\par (c) By choosing a suitable interval, show that \(\alpha=2.307\) correct to 3 decimal places. (3 marks)\par What are the rounding boundaries?
Lower boundary: \(2.3065\).
Upper boundary: \(2.3075\).
A root strictly between these boundaries rounds to 2.307 to 3 decimal places.
\[g(2.3065)=-0.000275221\ldots<0,\]\[g(2.3075)=0.004419850\ldots>0.\]There is a change of sign, and \(g\) is continuous. Thus\[2.3065<\alpha<2.3075.\]Therefore \(\alpha=2.307\) to 3 decimal places.

transcription.tex: (a) Using the same axes, sketch the graphs of \(y=\ln x\) and \(y=\frac{1}{x}\). Explain how your diagrams shows that the function \(y=\ln \left(x\right)-\frac{1}{x}\) has only one root.\par (b) Show that this root lies in the interval \(1.7<x<1.8\)\par (c) Given that the root of \(f\left(x\right)\) is \(\alpha \), show that \(\alpha =1.763\) correct to 3 decimal places.
Intersections satisfy \(\ln x=1/x\), hence \(f(x)=0\). The logarithm increases and the reciprocal decreases for \(x>0\); they meet once.
\[f(1.7)=-0.057607\ldots<0,\]\[f(1.8)=0.032231\ldots>0.\]Continuity and a sign change give a root in \((1.7,1.8)\).

transcription.tex: Question 2

\(f(x)=3+x^2-x^3\).\par (a) Show that the equation \(f(x)=0\) has a root, \(\alpha\), in the interval \([1.8,1.9]\).\par (b) By considering a change of sign of \(f(x)\) in a suitable interval, verify that \(\alpha=1.864\) correct to 3 decimal places.

(a) \[f(1.8)=3+1.8^2-1.8^3\]\[=0.40800000\ldots,\]\[f(1.9)=3+1.9^2-1.9^3\]\[=-0.24900000\ldots.\]The values have opposite signs, and the function is continuous on the interval. Hence a root lies between 1.8 and 1.9.

(b) Test the rounding boundaries:\[f(1.8635)=3+1.8635^2-1.8635^3\]\[=0.00138205\ldots,\]\[f(1.8645)=3+1.8645^2-1.8645^3\]\[=-0.00531344\ldots.\]There is a change of sign. Continuity gives \(1.8635<\alpha<1.8645\), so \(\alpha=1.864\) to 3 decimal places.

transcription.tex: Question 3

\(h(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}-\cos x-1\), where \(x\) is in radians.\par (a) Show that the equation \(h(x)=0\) has a root, \(\alpha\), between \(x=1.4\) and \(x=1.5\).\par (b) By choosing a suitable interval, show that \(\alpha=1.441\) is correct to 3 decimal places.

(a) \[h(1.4)=\sqrt[3]{1.4}-\cos1.4-1\]\[=-0.05127820\ldots,\]\[h(1.5)=\sqrt[3]{1.5}-\cos1.5-1\]\[=0.07397704\ldots.\]The values have opposite signs, and the function is continuous on the interval. Hence a root lies between 1.4 and 1.5.

(b) Test the rounding boundaries:\[h(1.4405)=\sqrt[3]{1.4405}-\cos1.4405-1\]\[=-0.00055404\ldots,\]\[h(1.4415)=\sqrt[3]{1.4415}-\cos1.4415-1\]\[=0.00069882\ldots.\]There is a change of sign. Continuity gives \(1.4405<\alpha<1.4415\), so \(\alpha=1.441\) to 3 decimal places.

transcription.tex: Question 4

\(f(x)=\sin x-\ln x\), \(x>0\), where \(x\) is in radians.\par (a) Show that \(f(x)=0\) has a root, \(\alpha\), in the interval \([2.2,2.3]\).\par (b) By considering a change of sign of \(f(x)\) in a suitable interval, verify that \(\alpha=2.219\) correct to 3 decimal places.

(a) \[f(2.2)=\sin2.2-\ln2.2\]\[=0.02003904\ldots,\]\[f(2.3)=\sin2.3-\ln2.3\]\[=-0.08720391\ldots.\]The values have opposite signs, and the function is continuous on the interval. Hence a root lies between 2.2 and 2.3.

(b) Test the rounding boundaries:\[f(2.2185)=\sin2.2185-\ln2.2185\]\[=0.00064011\ldots,\]\[f(2.2195)=\sin2.2195-\ln2.2195\]\[=-0.00041430\ldots.\]There is a change of sign. Continuity gives \(2.2185<\alpha<2.2195\), so \(\alpha=2.219\) to 3 decimal places.

slides.title: Using Iteration to Approximate a Root

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C3 January 2013}\par \(g(x)=e^{x-1}+x-6\).\par (a) Show that the equation \(g(x)=0\) can be written as \(x=\ln(6-x)+1\), \(x<6\). (2 marks)\par The root of \(g(x)=0\) is \(\alpha\). The iterative formula \(x_{n+1}=\ln(6-x_n)+1\), \(x_0=2\), is used to find an approximate value for \(\alpha\).\par (b) Calculate the values of \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) to 4 decimal places. (3 marks)\par (c) By choosing a suitable interval, show that \(\alpha=2.307\) correct to 3 decimal places. (3 marks)
\textbf{Iteration rule}\par Rearrange \(f(x)=0\) into \(x=g(x)\), then use \(x_{n+1}=g(x_n)\). We will see why this works shortly.
\textbf{Tip}\par There may be several occurrences of \(x\) to isolate. Use the target equation to guide the rearrangement.

(2 marks)\par The root of \(g(x)=0\) is \(\alpha\). The iterative formula \(x_{n+1}=\ln(6-x_n)+1\), \(x_0=2\), is used to find an approximate value for \(\alpha\).\par (b) Calculate the values of \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) to 4 decimal places. transcription.tex: The starting value matters: iteration can approach a different root, or fail to converge. Staircase and cobweb diagrams help explain why.\par \(f(x)=x^3-3x^2-2x+5\).\par a. Show there is a root in \(3<x<4\).\par b. Use \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{(x_n^3-2x_n+5)/3}\) to find \(x_1,x_2,x_3\), to 4 d.p., starting from i. \(x_0=1.5\); ii. \(x_0=4\).
\[f(3)=-1,\qquad f(4)=13.\]There is a change of sign, and \(f\) is continuous. Hence a root lies in \((3,4)\).
\[x_1=\sqrt{\frac{1.5^3-2(1.5)+5}{3}}=1.3385,\]\[x_2=1.2545,\quad x_3=1.2200.\]The changes become smaller; this sequence appears to converge to a different root.
\[x_1=4.5092,\quad x_2=5.4058,\]\[x_3=7.1219\quad\text{(4 d.p.).}\]The values grow away from the root: this iteration diverges.

(3 marks)\par The equation \(x^3+3x^2+4x-12=0\) has a single root which is between 1 and 2.\par (b) Use the iteration formula \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{4(3-x_n)/(3+x_n)}\), \(n\ge0\), with \(x_0=1\) to find, to 2 decimal places, the value of \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\). (3 marks)\par The root of \(f(x)=0\) is \(\alpha\).\par (c) By choosing a suitable interval, prove that \(\alpha=1.272\) to 3 decimal places. (3 marks)
\textbf{Exam tip}\par Mark schemes show the minimum acceptable wording. State the endpoint values, change of sign and continuity clearly.

transcription.tex: Solve \(x^2-x-1=0\). For the positive root, rearrange as \(x=\sqrt{x+1}\) and use \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{x_n+1}\). Why does this work?
The solution of \(x=\sqrt{x+1}\) is the intersection of \(y=x\) and \(y=\sqrt{x+1}\). Its \(x\)-coordinate, \(\alpha\), is a root of the original equation.
With \(x_0=1\), find \(\sqrt{x_0+1}\): move vertically to the curve to obtain the \(y\)-value.
This gives \(x_1=\sqrt2=1.414\ldots\). Feed it back as the next input: move horizontally to \(y=x\), so the \(y\)-value becomes the new \(x\)-value.
Repeat using \(x_1=1.414\ldots\) to obtain \(x_2\), and so on.
The staircase shape gives the name: a staircase diagram. The iterates converge towards \(\alpha\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Another rearrangement of \(x^2-x-1=0\) is \(x=1/(x-1)\). Use \(x_{n+1}=1/(x_n-1)\). What happens?
Start with a negative value, as in this diagram. Alternate between the curve \(y=1/(x-1)\) and the line \(y=x\).
The terms alternate around \(\alpha\) and move closer to it. This is a cobweb diagram. Here iteration converges to the negative root, \(\alpha=(1-\sqrt5)/2\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: We can also rearrange \(x^2-x-1=0\) as \(x=x^2-1\), giving \(x_{n+1}=x_n^2-1\). What happens now?
Start to the right of the positive root. Each iteration moves farther from \(\alpha\), instead of closer. The approximations diverge, so this attempt fails.

transcription.tex: \(f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}-8x+4\)\par (a) Show that the root of the equation \(f\left(x\right)=0\) can be written as \(x=\sqrt{8x-4}\)\par (b) Using the iterative formula \({x}_{n+1}=\sqrt{8{x}_{n}-4}\), and starting with \({x}_{0}=1\), draw a staircase diagram, indicating \({x}_{0},{x}_{1}, {x}_{2}\) on your \(x\)-axis, as well as the root \(\alpha \).

transcription.tex: Question 3

\(f(x)=x^2-6x+1\).\par (a) Show that the equation \(f(x)=0\) can be written as \(x=\sqrt{6x-1}\).\par (b) Sketch on the same axes the graphs of \(y=x\) and \(y=\sqrt{6x-1}\).\par (c) Write down the number of roots of \(f(x)\).\par (d) Use your diagram to explain why the iterative formula \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{6x_n-1}\) converges to a root of \(f(x)\) when \(x_0=2\).\par \(f(x)=0\) can also be rearranged to form the iterative formula \(x_{n+1}=(x_n^2+1)/6\).\par (e) By sketching a diagram, explain why the iteration diverges when \(x_0=10\).
(a) \[x^2-6x+1=0\Rightarrow x^2=6x-1.\]Both roots are positive, so take the positive square root: \(x=\sqrt{6x-1}\).
(c) The curve meets the line twice: there are two roots.
(d) Starting at 2, the staircase approaches the larger fixed point \(3+2\sqrt2\). Hence the iteration converges to this root.
3e conclusion Starting at 10, the steps move to larger values, farther from the fixed points. This iteration diverges.

transcription.tex: Solve \(f(x)=0\). Choose a starting value \(x_0\).
Locate \((x_0,f(x_0))\) on the curve.
The tangent meets the \(x\)-axis at \(x_1\).
\(\displaystyle \text{Gradient}=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}=\frac{f(x_0)}{x_0-x_1}\)
\(\displaystyle f^{\prime}(x_0)=\frac{f(x_0)}{x_0-x_1}\)
\(\displaystyle f(x_0)=(x_0-x_1)f^{\prime}(x_0)\)
\(\displaystyle \boxed{x_1=x_0-\frac{f(x_0)}{f^{\prime}(x_0)}}\)

transcription.tex: Repeat the process to obtain the iterative formula.

The function and its derivative must be defined, with \(f^{\prime}(x_n)\ne0\).

transcription.tex: Use Newton–Raphson to solve \(f(x)=x^3+x^2-5x+2=0\).
\(\displaystyle f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2+2x-5\)
\(\displaystyle x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f^{\prime}(x_n)}\)
\(\displaystyle x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{x_n^3+x_n^2-5x_n+2}{3x_n^2+2x_n-5}\)
\textbf{Calculator hint}\par Enter the recurrence using Ans in place of \(x_n\), then press EXE repeatedly.

transcription.tex: Also known as Newton’s method. We wish to find the root \(\alpha\). Start with an approximation \(x_0\), which may be well off the mark.
Follow the direction of the curve using its tangent. If the curve were reasonably straight, the point where the tangent hits the \(x\)-axis would be close to the root.

transcription.tex: At \(x=x_n\), the tangent has gradient \(f^{\prime}(x_n)\).
Using Year 1 coordinate geometry:
\[y-f(x_n)=f^{\prime}(x_n)(x-x_n).\]
At the tangent’s intersection with the axis, \(y=0\) and \(x=x_{n+1}\).
\[x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f^{\prime}(x_n)}.\]

transcription.tex: Return to \(x=\cos x\), with \(x_0=0.5\). Use radians: the differentiation formula assumes radian measure.

transcription.tex: The price of a car in £s, \(x\) years after purchase, is modelled by the function\par \(f\left(x\right)=15 000 {\left(0.85\right)}^{x}-1000\sin x,\hspace{1.12em}x>0\)\par (a) Use the model to find the value, to the nearest hundred £s, of the car 10 years after purchase.\par (b) Show that \(f\left(x\right)\) has a root between 19 and 20.\par (c) Find \({f}^{\prime }\left(x\right)\)\par (d) Taking 19.5 as a first approximation, apply the Newton-Raphson method once to \(f(x)\) to obtain a second approximation for the time when the value of the car is zero. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.\par (e) Criticise this model with respect to the value of the car as it gets older.
\[f(10)=3497.13\ldots\]The predicted value is £3500.
\[f(19)=534.114515\ldots>0,\]\[f(20)=-331.55\ldots<0.\]Continuity and the sign change give a root in \((19,20)\).
The model can predict negative prices, which are not meaningful car values. It is not reasonable for cars around 20 years old or older.
\[f(19.5)=25.0693\ldots,\quad f^{\prime}(19.5)=-898.3009\ldots\]\[x_1=19.5-\frac{f(19.5)}{f^{\prime}(19.5)}=19.527907\ldots\]The second approximation is 19.528 years.

transcription.tex: Question 1

An astronomer is studying the motion of a planet moving along an elliptical orbit. She formulates the following model relating the angle moved at a given time, \(E\) radians, to the angle the planet would have moved if it had been travelling on a circular path, \(M\) radians:\par \(M=E-0.1\sin E,\quad E\ge0.\)\par In order to predict the position of the planet at a particular time, the astronomer needs to find the value of \(E\) when \(M=\pi/6\).\par (a) Show that this value of \(E\) is a root of the function \(f(x)=x-0.1\sin x-k\) where \(k\) is a constant to be determined.\par (b) Taking 0.6 as a first approximation, apply the Newton–Raphson procedure once to \(f(x)\) to obtain a second approximation for the value of \(E\) when \(M=\pi/6\).\par (c) By considering a change of sign on a suitable interval of \(f(x)\), show that your answer to part (b) is correct to 3 decimal places.
(a) \[\frac\pi6=E-0.1\sin E\]\[E-0.1\sin E-\frac\pi6=0.\]Hence \(k=\pi/6\).

(c) \[f(0.5775)=0.5775-0.1\sin0.5775-\pi/6\]\[=-0.000692\ldots<0,\]\[f(0.5785)=0.5785-0.1\sin0.5785-\pi/6\]\[=0.000224361\ldots>0.\]The function is continuous and changes sign between the rounding boundaries. Hence \(E=0.578\) to 3 d.p.
